# Pseudonymise identifiers {#sec-uc-privacy}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_setup.R")
```

Linking data held by different organisations often means sharing
identifiers that should not leave the building: tax file numbers, Medicare
numbers, names and dates of birth. The usual answer is to replace each
identifier with a **pseudonym** -- a value that is the same every time the
same identifier goes in, so records still join, but that cannot be turned
back into the identifier. `fhash()` computes the digests this needs, over
whole columns and on every core.

This chapter is about using hashing *correctly* for that purpose. Hashing is
one control among several -- access rules, separation of duties, output
checking -- not a substitute for them.

## Why an unkeyed hash is not a pseudonym

A plain SHA-256 digest looks opaque, but most identifiers come from a small,
structured space. Anyone who knows the format can hash every possible value
and look the digest up. A million 9-digit candidates take a moment:

```{r}
#| label: brute-force
candidates <- sprintf("%09d", 0:999999)
system.time(digests <- fhash(candidates))

leaked <- fhash("000654321")          # a digest from a "de-identified" file
candidates[match(leaked, digests)]    # ...is an identifier again
```

At that rate the whole 9-digit space -- every possible TFN -- is a lunch
break on one laptop; most of the time above is R allocating the result
strings, and dedicated hardware computes billions of digests a second.
Names and dates of birth are an even smaller space. So an unkeyed hash of an
identifier is, for privacy purposes, the identifier.

## Keyed hashing (HMAC)

Give `fhash()` a secret `key` and it computes an HMAC instead (RFC 2104).
Without the key nobody can compute the pseudonym of a guessed identifier,
so the dictionary attack above fails; with it, the same identifier always
gets the same pseudonym:

```{r}
#| label: hmac
key <- "a long random secret held only by the linkage unit"
fhash(c("123456782", "123456782", "987654321"), key = key)
```

Generate the key randomly (for example `openssl::rand_bytes(32)`, which
`fhash()` accepts as a raw vector), keep it out of code and version
control, and give it only to the people who must compute pseudonyms. Two
custodians who hash with the same key can send their pseudonymised
extracts to a linkage unit that never sees an identifier, and that unit can
join them exactly.

## Normalise before you hash

Hashing is exact: one character of difference gives an unrelated digest.
Formatting differences that a human would ignore therefore break the join,
unless every party normalises the same way first:

```{r}
#| label: normalise
raw <- c("123456782", "123 456 782", "123-456-782")
fhash(raw, key = key)                                  # three pseudonyms
fhash(fgsub("[^0-9]", "", raw), key = key)             # one pseudonym
```

Write the normalisation down and share it with the key. For names that
means case, accents, punctuation and whitespace at least
(`toupper()`, `ascii_fold()`, `fgsub()`, `fsquish()`), and often nicknames
and titles too (`freplace_tokens()`, @sec-uc-clean). Validate identifiers
before hashing (`valid_id()`, @sec-uc-profile): a mistyped number hashes to a
pseudonym that will never match anything.

## Linkage keys from names and dates of birth

Where there is no shared identifier, a *statistical linkage key* built from
name fragments, date of birth and sex stands in for one. In Australian
health and community-services data the standard is the AIHW's SLK-581:
letters 2, 3 and 5 of the family name, letters 2 and 3 of the given name,
the date of birth as `DDMMYYYY` and a sex code. A sketch of the core rules,
built from vectorised pieces, then hashed with the key:

```{r}
#| label: slk581
slk_letters <- function(name, positions, missing) {
    letters_only <- fgsub("[^A-Z]", "", toupper(ascii_fold(name)))
    # short names are padded with "2"
    padded <- fpad(letters_only, max(positions), side = "right", pad = "2")
    out <- do.call(paste0, lapply(positions, function(p) fsubstr(padded, p, p)))
    out[is.na(name) | !nzchar(letters_only)] <- missing
    out
}
slk581 <- function(family, given, dob, sex) {
    paste0(slk_letters(family, c(2, 3, 5), "999"),
           slk_letters(given, c(2, 3), "99"),
           fgsub("/", "", format_date(dob, "dmy"), fixed = TRUE),
           sex)
}

people <- data.frame(
    family = c("O'Brien", "Smith", "Ng", "Smith-Jones", NA),
    given  = c("Mary", "Jo", "Li", "Bill", "Ann"),
    dob    = as.Date(c("1985-03-15", "1990-07-22", "1975-12-01", "1988-01-05",
                       "2000-02-29")),
    sex    = c(2, 1, 9, 1, 2)
)
people$slk <- slk581(people$family, people$given, people$dob, people$sex)
people$pseudonym <- fhash(people$slk, key = key)
people[, c("family", "given", "slk", "pseudonym")]
```

The AIHW specification has further rules (for example for names given only
as initials) -- follow it for production use. An SLK is coarse by design:
different people can share one, and one person's key changes with a change
of surname, so treat matches on it as evidence, not proof.

## Fast fingerprints for change detection

Not every hash needs to be secret. XXH64 is a fast, non-cryptographic
64-bit hash: useful for spotting which rows changed between two extracts,
partitioning data or building compact join keys. Hash each row's fields
joined with a separator that cannot occur in the data:

```{r}
#| label: change-detection
old <- data.frame(id = 1:5, name = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
                  addr = c("1 X St", "2 Y St", "3 Z St", "4 W St", "5 V St"))
new <- old
new$addr[c(2, 5)] <- c("22 Y St", "5 V Street")
new <- rbind(new, data.frame(id = 6, name = "F", addr = "6 U St"))

row_hash <- function(df) fhash(do.call(paste, c(df, sep = "\x1f")), "xxh64")
new$id[!row_hash(new) %in% row_hash(old)]     # rows that are new or changed
```

## Which algorithm

| Purpose | Use |
|---|---|
| Pseudonyms for sharing or linking | `fhash(x, "sha256", key = key)` (or `"sha512"`) |
| Matching an existing hashed dataset | whatever it used -- often unkeyed SHA-256, or MD5/SHA-1 for older data |
| Change detection, partitioning, compact keys | `fhash(x, "xxh64")` |

MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for collision resistance; use them only to match
data that is already hashed that way. Digests agree with `openssl` and
`digest`, so pseudonyms computed here can be reproduced elsewhere -- and
strings are hashed as UTF-8, so the result does not depend on how R happens
to store the text.
